They ditched it because command line/terminal is a horrible unfriendly user interface. It's opaque, it doesn't tell you what your options are, it doesn't provide feedback of any kind, and it requires a memorized knowledge of proper commands and syntax. Over the last 10-15 years of trying Linux distros, I've come to believe this is a problem that will never be solved. Watching distros evolved, as they upgrade the gui, new icons, fancy animations, adding docks, changing screen layouts, I can see that thousands of hours have been poured into improving these operating systems. Additionally there's very poor documentation and a lack of help menus.

I think it's an inherent problem with a large open source project that relies on volunteers. And it will never go away. Everyone wants to work on the exciting fun things like animation graphics for pop up menus or new icon packs or desktop layouts, but no one wants to work on the boring stuff like making comprehensive Options menus, or writing 20 pages of documentation...

After all these years, Linux still feels like an unfinished Operating System.

This comment will probably be buried, but as a recent Linux convert, I wanted to add my 2c.

Despite what some people will have you believe, switching to Linux is not as easy as they would make it seem. There are a lot of points to consider, and you're going to run into teething problems that require a certain, investigative mindset in order to resolve them, even with the more User Friendly distros like Ubuntu.

Not everyone has the patience for it, and many Win and Mac Users just want shit to work and very rarely will be willing to do the amount of troubleshooting required to resolve some of the issue they may encounter on Linux.

That said, most of the traditional roadblocks that have existed to prevent Linux being a viable alternative to most people, are now being eroded.

The biggest one by far is Gaming, and yet that is now becoming less of an issue with services like Steam and GOG supporting Linux and a larger library of games being ported over. Proprietary drivers from AMD and Nvidia are improving, and with the release of Vulkan as a potential rival for DirectX, the future of gaming is going to be radically different from where it is now.

My advice to those who have raised concerns, install a Linux distro in a VM. Play around with it. See what alternative programs are available for what you do on your current OS. You don't have to switch, but it is never a good idea to keep yourself ignorant of potential options, just because you are more comfortable where you are at the time.

What are the advantages of space-to-sea barge landings? Honest question, I zero spaceship knowledge.

tl;dr it saves fuel.

The barge lets them land the rocket anywhere they want, as long as it's at sea. This means they don't need to fly the rocket as far, which means they can carry less fuel for landing, which in turn lets them carry more payload.

There was no other option for this mission. The orbit they needed to get this payload to meant not having enough fuel leftover to do a boost back burn on the 1st stage (bringing it back in the direction of the launch site) in addition to the other burns needed for the landing. So, after 1st stage engine shutdown and separation, the stage continued on it's path ballistically. They used cold-gas thrusters to flip it so it was would be heading back in engines first. They did a short re-entry burn to slow it a bit, and then a landing burn. It's actually impressive they got as close as they did given the options here. The barge was somewhere around 668km out in the Atlantic.

They need to get barge landings to work because they won't always have the option to bring it back to land. All launches go out over water. If it's from the Cape, they go out over the Atlantic. If it's from Vandenberg, then it's the Pacific. Eventually SpaceX will have a launch site in south Texas and then it'll be out over the Gulf. Missions that require high orbits leave less fuel for the 1st stage landings. In those cases, sea landings are the only option.

Space is hard. No one that knows what is actually involved, even a little bit, will think them incompetent. This is an incredibly hard thing to do.
